frictionVectors.title: European gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control through Sonatrach while expanding gas ties with Italy and other European buyers. External pressure centers on supply reliability, pricing, and investment access.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya raises border-security costs and complicates Algeria's preference for non-intervention and diplomatic mediation.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese-linked infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Angola is diversifying from heavy Chinese financing but remains exposed to debt, construction, and commodity-linked infrastructure relationships. The Lobito Corridor has intensified competition among Western, Gulf, and Chinese interests.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector dependency
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues remain central to fiscal stability, limiting sovereign flexibility when prices or production decline. International oil majors retain substantial influence over capital-intensive offshore projects.

frictionVectors.title: Northern jihadist spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity moving south from the Sahel threatens northern communities, transport routes, and protected areas. Benin is strengthening partnerships with regional and external security providers while seeking to preserve operational autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou's trade role and major infrastructure projects attract Chinese, regional, and Gulf-linked capital. This expands connectivity but creates exposure to external financing terms and shifting relations with Nigeria and landlocked neighbors.

frictionVectors.title: Debswana bargaining pressure
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is using its diamond resources and state partnership with De Beers to secure greater local value, marketing power, and downstream activity. The main risk is reduced global diamond demand weakening negotiating leverage.

frictionVectors.title: New mineral investment race
frictionVectors.details: Copper, uranium, and other strategic minerals are attracting foreign investors seeking long-term access. Botswana's regulatory stability provides leverage, but limited domestic processing capacity keeps external firms influential.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector sovereignty drive
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking tighter state control over gold production, refining, and marketing while challenging foreign mining arrangements. Insecurity and limited technical capacity complicate efforts to convert resource nationalism into reliable public revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Security dependence and sanctions risk
frictionVectors.details: The deepening relationship with Russia and reported reliance on Russian-linked security support reduce dependence on Western partners but introduce reputational, sanctions, and accountability risks. Persistent militant violence continues to constrain infrastructure and extractive activity.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Investment Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking foreign capital and technical expertise to develop nickel and rare-earth potential, limiting near-term state control over strategic minerals.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Border Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Instability in eastern DRC and strained relations with Rwanda complicate trade routes, border security, and access to Lake Tanganyika infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Port, airport, and digital-connectivity projects depend heavily on European, Chinese, and multilateral financing, creating long-term exposure to outside creditors and operators.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security Burden
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's strategic Atlantic position brings foreign security partnerships and surveillance assistance while exposing its limited resources to transnational narcotics trafficking.

frictionVectors.title: Oil, Gas, and Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon, timber, and emerging mining sectors remain shaped by foreign firms and external capital, while weak transparency limits domestic capture of resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Damaged Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Anglophone conflict and insecurity in the Far North disrupt roads, agricultural supply chains, and energy expansion, increasing reliance on external security and infrastructure partners.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security-Mining Nexus
frictionVectors.details: Russian security involvement is closely associated with access to gold, diamonds, and other strategic commodities, reducing the transparency and bargaining power of state institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Unsecured Trade Routes
frictionVectors.details: Armed-group activity and weak transport infrastructure constrain national control over mining zones and border commerce, especially along routes toward Cameroon, Chad, and Sudan.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Oil Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal and strategic autonomy remains tied to oil exports, pipeline infrastructure, and foreign technical operators, leaving the state vulnerable to price shocks and contractual asymmetry.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Spillover and Security Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan conflict and wider Sahel insecurity strain border infrastructure and military capacity, encouraging reliance on external security relationships and limiting independent resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: French control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains administrative control of Mayotte, making the dispute a persistent sovereignty issue for Moroni. Maritime boundaries, migration, and access to surrounding resources remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: External financing constraints
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on diaspora remittances and external partners for infrastructure and public investment. Limited fiscal capacity restricts its ability to control strategic projects independently.

frictionVectors.title: Mining concessions and critical minerals
frictionVectors.details: Copper, cobalt, and other strategic minerals attract intense competition from Chinese, Western, and regional firms. Weak contract enforcement and limited domestic processing allow substantial value to leave the country.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern security and regional interference
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving armed groups and alleged external support continues to obstruct Kinshasa's control over territory and mineral corridors. Regional diplomacy has not yet produced durable security or supply-chain sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily dependent on oil production and external capital, leaving public finances exposed to price cycles and foreign operators. Domestic control over downstream value creation remains limited.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-finance exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain important in roads, construction, and resource-linked infrastructure. These partnerships expand capacity but can reduce transparency around debt, concessions, and long-term strategic control.

frictionVectors.title: External influence over strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: French, Chinese, Gulf, and other foreign investors compete across ports, transport, energy, and telecommunications. Côte d'Ivoire is diversifying partners, but foreign capital remains central to major infrastructure decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa processing and producer control
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater domestic processing and stronger producer bargaining power in cocoa and other commodities. Exposure to global buyers, financing conditions, and climate shocks still limits sovereign value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-base dependence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its location through foreign military facilities, including major American, Chinese, French, and other presences. This generates revenue and security but constrains strategic autonomy and increases exposure to rival-power competition.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt concentration
frictionVectors.details: Chinese involvement in ports, rail, and logistics has expanded Djibouti's infrastructure while intensifying concerns over debt exposure and control of strategic assets. Competition with regional ports adds further pressure on the country's economic model.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam remains Cairo's central strategic concern, with Egypt seeking enforceable operating rules and broader diplomatic leverage over upstream water management.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF programs, Gulf investment, and foreign borrowing stabilize the economy but increase outside influence over major infrastructure, currency, and privatization decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Maturing oil and gas fields
frictionVectors.details: Declining conventional production is tightening state revenues and encouraging renewed negotiations with foreign energy firms over offshore gas, recovery projects, and new exploration.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and resource-linked contracting remain important to Malabo, while debt exposure and limited transparency constrain independent control over national assets.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to shipping lanes attract competing Gulf, Turkish, Egyptian, and Western attention, increasing strategic value while exposing Asmara to pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-operated gold, copper, and zinc projects provide hard currency but leave the state reliant on external capital, technology, and opaque concession arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Regional corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini's access to ports, fuel, and manufactured imports depends heavily on South African and Mozambican transport networks, leaving it exposed to regional disruption.

frictionVectors.title: Political legitimacy pressure
frictionVectors.details: The monarchy's control over political institutions limits reform and can complicate relations with external donors, investors, and regional partners seeking stronger governance guarantees.

frictionVectors.title: Nile and GERD tensions
frictionVectors.details: The GERD strengthens Ethiopia's electricity and bargaining position, but unresolved operating arrangements with Egypt and Sudan continue to carry escalation risks.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict and infrastructure access
frictionVectors.details: Internal conflict, contested federal authority, and insecurity along key corridors threaten transport, telecoms, and energy assets while increasing reliance on foreign mediation and financing.

highlights: Transition government tightens control over oil and manganese

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The post-Bongo authorities are seeking greater state participation and transparency in oil, mining, and logging. Contract revisions could improve sovereign capture but risk deterring investors and provoking arbitration.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: Manganese exports remain dependent on transport corridors and port infrastructure linked to foreign operators and financing. Disruptions or renegotiations could quickly affect fiscal revenues.

highlights: Small-state autonomy constrained by external finance
Port and security links deepen foreign dependence

frictionVectors.title: Debt and donor leverage
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on IMF, World Bank, and bilateral support to stabilize public finances and fund infrastructure. This preserves macroeconomic access but limits room for independent policy choices.

frictionVectors.title: Port modernization competition
frictionVectors.details: Banjul port upgrades and maritime-security cooperation attract foreign contractors and strategic partners. The government must balance investment needs against concerns over long-term concessions and regional dependence.

highlights: Gold remains strategic but illicit mining erodes state control

frictionVectors.title: Galamsey and mining governance
frictionVectors.details: Illegal gold mining damages water systems and exposes weaknesses in enforcement, while foreign-linked supply chains capture value outside formal channels. Public pressure is pushing Accra toward tougher controls and greater domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: External stabilization conditions
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed reforms and debt restructuring are central to fiscal recovery. They improve access to financing but constrain subsidy, spending, and industrial-policy choices.

highlights: Bauxite wealth expands state bargaining power
Simandou raises sovereignty and infrastructure stakes

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore project is bringing major foreign capital, rail, and port infrastructure into Guinea. Its scale could transform state revenues, but consortium control and enclave-style logistics remain central sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: Junta and investor uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: The military government is using mining negotiations to assert control while delaying a full political transition. Contract uncertainty and limited institutional oversight increase the risk that resource gains remain concentrated and volatile.

highlights: Cashew dependence leaves the economy externally exposed
Political fragility limits control of strategic assets

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain capture
frictionVectors.details: Raw cashew exports dominate rural livelihoods and foreign exchange, while processing capacity remains limited. Traders and external buyers capture much of the value, leaving the state vulnerable to price and logistics shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Port, narcotics, and security networks
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and recurring political disruption make ports and maritime routes vulnerable to transnational trafficking and informal influence. External security and commercial actors can gain leverage when state oversight is fragmented.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressure limits Nairobi's policy autonomy and sustains reliance on Chinese, Gulf, and Western financing for transport and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Critical-Mineral Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and Lamu remain strategically contested gateways, while foreign firms are positioning for access to Kenya's emerging critical-mineral and renewable-energy sectors.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project Asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports provide vital revenue but deepen structural dependence on South Africa, which controls the primary downstream market and infrastructure relationship.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and Mining Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-owned textile production and diamond mining remain exposed to external demand, labor-cost shifts, and limited domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Iron-Ore Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: ArcelorMittal and other foreign operators retain major influence over mining, rail, and port arrangements, constraining Liberia's ability to capture more downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure Financing Competition
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia is balancing Western-backed governance support with Chinese and other foreign interest in roads, ports, energy, and extractive infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Oil Authorities
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed centers continue contesting control over the National Oil Corporation, export terminals, and revenue allocation.

frictionVectors.title: Turkish and Russian Security Footprints
frictionVectors.details: Foreign military and security involvement gives outside powers leverage over strategic corridors and energy assets, limiting Libya's sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Nickel and Cobalt
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed mining projects dominate strategic mineral production, while Madagascar remains vulnerable to price cycles and limited domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Logging and Land Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Illegal rosewood extraction and contested mining concessions weaken state authority, especially where enforcement capacity is limited and foreign demand remains strong.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Exchange and Fuel Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Persistent dollar shortages and reliance on imported fuel constrain policy autonomy. Debt restructuring and IMF conditions remain central to Malawi's economic sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Mining Negotiations
frictionVectors.details: Uranium, rare-earth and niobium projects offer diversification but require foreign capital. Weak bargaining capacity and limited processing infrastructure could leave Malawi capturing only a small share of resource value.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state participation and revenue from gold, creating repeated disputes with international operators. Production and investment remain vulnerable to regulatory uncertainty and insecurity.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Logistics Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian security personnel and equipment has reduced dependence on Western partners but increased strategic exposure to Moscow. Attacks on transport corridors and mining zones continue to undermine sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Senegal Gas-Field Coordination
frictionVectors.details: The shared Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers major revenue potential but requires sustained Mauritania-Senegal coordination on revenue, operations and maritime security. Delays or disputes could weaken expected fiscal gains.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Extractive Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and gas development depend heavily on foreign operators, financing and port infrastructure. Nouakchott is expanding local-content and processing ambitions, but remains exposed to commodity prices and external capital.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Implementation Risks
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago has advanced diplomatically, but implementation involving Diego Garcia remains sensitive. The issue tests relations with the United Kingdom, United States and India.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Connectivity Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is balancing Indian, Chinese, Gulf and Western interest in ports, logistics and digital infrastructure. The competition creates investment opportunities but raises risks of strategic dependence and pressure over maritime access.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Legitimacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate, fisheries, ports and renewable projects in Western Sahara remain central to Morocco's development strategy but contested by the Polisario Front and subject to legal scrutiny in European markets.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Drought, groundwater stress and dependence on imported energy constrain the benefits of Morocco's industrial expansion. Renewable investment and green-hydrogen partnerships improve resilience but remain reliant on foreign technology and capital.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado LNG Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators and security partners remain central to reviving the halted LNG project, limiting Mozambique's near-term bargaining power. Insurgent attacks continue to threaten transport links and local legitimacy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Maputo, Beira, and Nacala corridors attract competing regional and external investors. Revenue, customs control, and infrastructure concessions remain vulnerable to uneven state capacity.

highlights: Critical Minerals and Oil Drive Leverage

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital in Strategic Energy
frictionVectors.details: New oil, gas, uranium, and green-hydrogen projects could expand state revenue but are largely dependent on foreign finance, technology, and offtake agreements. Windfall expectations are increasing pressure for stronger local-content rules.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Namibia's trade and project logistics remain concentrated around Walvis Bay and regional transport links. External operators and neighboring-country demand give infrastructure partners meaningful influence over strategic corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiations
frictionVectors.details: The military authorities are seeking greater state control and revenue from uranium and other extractive projects, creating sustained tension with foreign operators. Production disruption and legal disputes could weaken near-term export earnings.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The withdrawal of Western forces has increased reliance on Russian security assistance while insurgent violence persists. This broadens Niger's diplomatic autonomy but risks substituting one external dependency for another.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Theft and Pipeline Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, sabotage, and weak infrastructure continue to reduce state capture of petroleum value despite efforts to raise production. Foreign operators and domestic security networks remain deeply embedded in the operating environment.

frictionVectors.title: Refinery and Gas Infrastructure Financing
frictionVectors.details: The Dangote refinery and planned gas projects improve Nigeria's strategic autonomy, but financing, feedstock access, and regulatory disputes remain significant. International lenders and energy firms retain leverage over expansion and export decisions.

highlights: Eastern Congo Ties Raise External Pressure

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Supply-Chain Scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's role as a minerals trading and processing hub is attracting intensified scrutiny over the origin and traceability of materials linked to eastern Congo. Western and regional pressure could affect access to premium markets and financing.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Security and Aid Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong state control over infrastructure and strategic sectors, but military involvement around eastern Congo exposes it to sanctions and donor pressure. Its security partnerships provide leverage while increasing diplomatic costs.

frictionVectors.title: UNCERTAIN HYDROCARBON FRONTIER
frictionVectors.details: Interest in the jointly managed offshore zone remains constrained by high exploration costs and uncertain commercial reserves. São Tomé and Príncipe has limited bargaining power against larger foreign energy firms.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Port, energy, and connectivity projects rely heavily on external partners, including Chinese and European financing. Debt capacity limits the government's ability to impose stronger sovereign conditions.

frictionVectors.title: OIL AND GAS CONTRACT RESET
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater state participation and tighter oversight of foreign-operated oil and gas projects, including the Senegal-Mauritania GTA development. Renegotiation risks investor friction and slower project execution.

frictionVectors.title: FISCAL SOVEREIGNTY PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Debt stress and disputes over public accounts constrain Dakar's ability to fund infrastructure without IMF support or external capital. Fiscal consolidation may collide with promises to retain more resource revenue domestically.

frictionVectors.title: TUNA ACCESS AND FISHERIES CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fleets and access agreements remain central to the economy, creating recurring concerns over licensing revenue, local value capture, and stock sustainability. Seychelles is strengthening monitoring but still depends on external markets and vessels.

frictionVectors.title: SMALL-STATE INFRASTRUCTURE EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Ports, digital connectivity, and climate-resilience projects require foreign finance and technical partners. The government must balance Indian, European, Chinese, and multilateral involvement without compromising strategic autonomy.

highlights: Port and rail corridors reshape leverage

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE AND MINERAL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining remains dominated by foreign capital and exposed to commodity-price swings, limiting domestic control over value chains. Freetown is pressing for local processing, higher fiscal returns, and stronger environmental enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: LOGISTICS CORRIDOR COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, rail, and mining infrastructure is increasing export capacity but can lock the country into enclave economics. Negotiations over concession terms and access fees remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: TURKEY-BACKED ENERGY EXPANSION
frictionVectors.details: Somalia's offshore oil framework and Turkish security and energy cooperation offer state-building potential but deepen dependence on an external strategic partner. Weak federal coordination and insecurity complicate licensing, revenue sharing, and environmental oversight.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND MARITIME RIVALRIES
frictionVectors.details: UAE-linked commercial interests, Turkish involvement, Gulf competition, and neighboring states' maritime claims continue to shape port infrastructure and access. Fragmented authority leaves Somalia vulnerable to deals that prioritize external leverage over national resource integration.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and port bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages, rail constraints, and port inefficiency limit South Africa's ability to convert mineral wealth into domestic industrial power. Foreign investors and trading partners are competing for access while Pretoria seeks greater local beneficiation.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: United States, China, and European actors are expanding engagement around platinum-group metals, manganese, and rare-earth supply chains. South Africa retains bargaining power but faces pressure to provide stable terms and infrastructure.

highlights: Oil lifeline exposed to regional war

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline dependence on Sudan
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's export revenues depend on pipelines and terminals in war-affected Sudan, leaving production vulnerable to sabotage, transit disruption, and bargaining pressure from external and regional actors.

frictionVectors.title: Externalized oil governance
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators, neighboring states, and international financial channels remain central to oil production and revenue management. Weak institutions and elite competition limit sovereign control over resource proceeds.

highlights: Red Sea access becomes strategic prize

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of oil infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: The conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces has disrupted transport, refining, and export networks. Armed factions and foreign backers are incentivized to control revenue-generating corridors rather than restore unified national management.

frictionVectors.title: Port and gold-route competition
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan and gold-producing areas are strategically important to rival domestic and external actors. Gulf, Egyptian, Russian, and regional interests increase the risk that infrastructure and mineral trade will be securitized and captured by competing networks.

frictionVectors.title: LNG bargaining and local-content pressure
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking stronger fiscal returns, domestic participation, and processing commitments from international gas developers. Delays in project agreements reflect an effort to preserve sovereignty while attracting the capital and technology required for export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and strategic corridors
frictionVectors.details: Upgrades at Dar es Salaam and competing regional corridors are drawing interest from China, Gulf investors, India, and Western partners. Infrastructure finance can expand national leverage but may also create long-term exposure to external lenders and operators.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional logistics hinge

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor influence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is central to Togo's trade and regional transit strategy, attracting foreign capital and commercial competition. Dependence on external operators, financing, and shipping networks limits full sovereign control over logistics infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Northern spillover insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence and instability moving south from the Sahel are increasing security costs around northern transport and resource corridors. Expanded foreign security assistance may strengthen state capacity while creating additional external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: European financial and border-management support gives the EU substantial leverage over Tunisian migration policy. Disputes over funding, migrant protection, and sovereignty remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Phosphate Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported energy and constrained phosphate production, limiting fiscal autonomy. External financing needs and investment conditions continue to shape strategic infrastructure decisions.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Sanctions Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The East African Crude Oil Pipeline remains central to Uganda's resource strategy but faces financing, environmental, and sanctions-related pressure from Western governments and civil-society groups. Uganda is relying more heavily on state-backed and non-Western partners.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Backed Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign lenders remain important to transport and energy construction. Debt-service obligations can narrow Kampala's policy space while major projects prioritize export connectivity.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Copper Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking greater domestic value addition and fiscal returns from copper, but foreign firms still dominate capital, technology, and export channels. Competition among Chinese, Gulf, Western, and regional investors gives Lusaka leverage but also creates regulatory pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Power Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring has improved Zambia's room for maneuver, yet creditors and international financial institutions continue to influence fiscal policy. Electricity shortages and weak transmission infrastructure threaten mining expansion and industrialization.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Mining Dominance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese companies remain deeply embedded in Zimbabwe's lithium, platinum, and infrastructure sectors. Harare's bargaining position is strengthened by mineral demand but weakened by limited access to finance, technology, and transparent enforcement capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and Debt Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions, arrears, and restricted capital-market access push Zimbabwe toward non-Western investors and opaque bilateral arrangements. The resulting dependence can reduce the state's ability to secure fair terms for strategic minerals and infrastructure.
